title: Burst capacity guardrails and autoscaling policy — Customer Omega
content:
Purpose:
Quick working note for the Customer Omega POC: propose a conservative but operationally simple autoscaling and burst-guardrail design for Dedicated GPU pools. Focus is on predictable tail-latency SLOs, cost headroom for bursts, and clear knobs for CS/ops during demos and ramp.

Context and constraints:
- Customer Omega: interactive product with spiky traffic (marketing-triggered bursts + business-hours steady). Expected 95th percentile request size ~350 tokens, 99th ~1200 tokens.
- Business requirement: 95th-percentile generation latency < 400ms for L1 flows, L2 flows can tolerate 1s.
- Security: Dedicated pool (customer-owned VPC overlay) but Redwood manages autoscaling and prewarming.
- Budget constraint: baseline reserved monthly commit for GPU hours equivalent to 3x average steady-state; additional burst must be cost-capped.

Traffic profile (empirical input):
- Avg RPS (steady): 6 requests/sec (mixed L1/L2), peak burst up to 85 RPS for short windows (10-30s) during promotional events.
- Token distribution: median 120, p95 350, p99 1200.
- Inference model: primary is M-13B quantized to 4-bit (Q4), fallback to S-7B Q4 for overloads.

SLOs and objectives:
- Objective A: keep L1 95p latency < 400ms 99% of the time outside of documented burst windows.
- Objective B: avoid >20% unseen error-rate or throttling during short bursts (10-30s); allow graceful degradation to S-7B.
- Objective C: limit incremental burst spend to <$5k per month above reserved commit during POC.

Proposed capacity mapping (baseline):
- Reserved pool: 4 x GPU-H100-80GB-equivalent nodes (logical capacity). This handles steady traffic with a safety factor 3 on average load. Rationale: customer requires predictable baseline for conversational flows.
- Elastic burst buffer: separate auto-scaling group with smaller cheaper GPUs (A100-40GB or mixed A100/H100 fractional slices) to absorb transient peaks and to run warm standby S-7B replicas.

Autoscaling policy (guardrail-first):
1) Fast up, conservative down:
   - Scale-up trigger: when 95th latency > 350ms OR queue depth > 25 for > 4s, start 1 GPU add. Allow immediate add up to 4 GPUs (to react to large burst).
   - Scale-down cooldown: require sustained low load for 6 minutes before removing a GPU. Remove max 1 GPU per cooldown to avoid oscillation.
2) Prewarm hooks for predictable bursts:
   - If incoming RPS increases > 30% vs 1-min baseline and trend > 3 consecutive 10s samples, prewarm 1 elastic GPU (no longer than 1 GPU per 15s sample).
3) Graceful degradation policy (quality-first):
   - If total queue > 200 requests or average wait time > 2s, shift majority of new requests to S-7B routing (automated fallback).
   - Persist 1 S-7B replica in reserved pool as absolute fallback (cold-start avoided).
4) Hard budget guardrail:
   - Elastic spend throttle: if projected incremental spend for burst pool in current billing day > 25% of daily burst budget, begin rejecting non-critical requests and notify CS/ops. (Daily budget computed from monthly burst cap).

Prewarm and KV cache strategy:
- Keep KV cache warm across reserved pool for hot sessions: persist top-200 session caches in memory on reserved nodes.
- Elastic nodes will fetch KV from reserved nodes on handover; expect ~50ms extra warmup on first request.

Cost modeling (quick run-rate estimates for POC):
Assumptions and unit costs (rough pricing, adjust to procurement):
- H100 equivalent (fully-managed bare node): $14.00 / hr (usage rate)
- A100-40GB equivalent: $6.50 / hr
- Operator overhead (OS, container, scheduler): ~8% on top of GPU cost in our model
- Reserved commit: assume 720 hrs / month per node.

Baseline monthly reserved cost (4 x H100-eq):
- GPU usage: 4 * 720 * $14 = $40,320
- Operator overhead: 8% = $3,226
- Total reserved ~ $43,546 / month

Burst-run incremental cost (example realistic burst pattern):
- Typical event: 3 bursts / month, each 20s median at 85 RPS (sustained for 20s), plus tail post-processing 5 minutes at 25 RPS. Assume autoscale adds 4 A100s for 30s and 2 A100s for 5 minutes.
- Event GPU-seconds: (4 A100 * 30s) + (2 A100 * 300s) = 120s + 600s = 720 GPU-seconds = 0.2 GPU-hrs per event (per A100-equivalent accounting).
- With 3 events: 0.6 GPU-hrs overall. Cost at $6.5/hr = $3.90. Operator overhead ~ $0.31. Clearly tiny — major cost driver is longer sustained bursts and overprovisioning.

Sensitivity scenarios to watch:
- Longer bursts (5–20 minutes) increase cost linearly; a 10-minute sustained extra 4 A100s costs ~ 4 * (10/60) * $6.5 = ~$4.33 — still modest per event but adds up for many events.
- If H100 reserved nodes are underutilized and elastic nodes are used as primary, switching more to cheaper A100s (or fractional sharing) reduces cost 30–50% but needs careful latency testing.

Example per-token economics (rough, for ops discussions):
- Assume M-13B Q4 inference cost (GPU time) averages 3.2ms/token on H100 equiv. If H100 cost is $14/hr -> $14 / 3600 = $0.003888.../sec. At 3.2ms/token, cost_per_token_gpu = 0.003888*0.0032 = ~$0.0000124 per token. Add overheads, rounding -> ~$0.000016/token.
- For p95 request (350 tokens) cost ~ $0.0056 per request (GPU only), plus infra and SLO overhead -> budget ~ $0.007–$0.01 / request.

Operational runbook (short):
- During demo windows: CS toggles "Burst Mode" in console to increase elastic budget cap by 2x for scheduled time window. This bypasses hard guardrail but logs escalation to pagerOps.
- If latency climbs and autoscale fails to converge in 90s: switch routing to S-7B fallback manually (ops button) and open incident ticket (JIRA SE-3421).
- Post-event: run a quick retrospective, collect traces and token histograms for threshold tuning.

Risk and open questions (action items):
- Q1: Thundering herd risk on cache warming for elastic nodes. ACTION: Maya to prototype a warming handshake that prefetches top-k KV for new node (ticket: GH #812).
- Q2: Pricing accuracy for H100/A100 slices — procurement to confirm negotiated committed rates (Carlos).
- Q3: Behavioural model for request routing when several fallbacks are available (S-7B vs quantized variants) — need eval harness for quality delta metric (Evelyn).

Next steps (owners):
- Prototype autoscale policy in staging with a synthetic burst generator (Riley + Maya) — target by 2025-02-25.
- Run cost-sensitivity table for committed vs burst mix (Carlos) — deliver by 2025-03-01.
- Build a short demo workflow for CS to flip Burst Mode and observe guardrail effects (Evelyn) — demo ready 2025-03-10.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep initial POC conservative: prefer slightly underprepared bursts with clear fallback to more compact model rather than aggressive overprovisioning.
- Document exact metric names in Console (latency_95_ms, queue_depth, elastic_cost_day) before handover to CS.

References and quick links:
- Incident playbook: Confluence /pages/viewpage.action?pageId=44332211
- Simulation harness: GH repo infra/tools/burst-sim
- Related sizing notes: see shared_drives/engineering/solutions-engineering-and-professional-services/prewarm-demand-forecast-pool-proposal.json (for baseline forecasts)

---
End of working note. Keep iterations in this doc; will fold into a final POC proposal once we have staging sim numbers.
